passage:
“Still not submitted?” Sumit asked from the top bunk, peering down at Chetan's laptop.
“It's basically done,” Chetan said.
“You said that on the ninth. It's the twenty-eighth.”
“Just the last polish. The cover page, the references.”
“That's twenty minutes.”
Chetan shut the lid halfway. “What if Sir hates it? What if the second chapter is weak?”
“Then he says so, and you fix it. Right now he can't say anything, because he hasn't got it.”
Chetan was quiet. Then he opened the laptop, fixed the cover page, pasted the references, and his finger hovered over the submit button.
“Go on,” said Sumit.
Click. Chetan exhaled as if he'd been holding his breath for weeks.

qa.q: On which date did Chetan say the project was basically done?
qa.a: Chetan said it was basically done on the ninth, and by the twenty-eighth it still was not submitted.

qa.q: What was Chetan afraid of when he shut the lid halfway?
qa.a: Chetan was afraid the second chapter was weak and that Sir would hate the work, so he felt anxious about being judged.

qa.q: What small steps did Chetan take to finish, in order?
qa.a: Chetan fixed the cover page, pasted the references and then pressed submit while Sumit encouraged him.

qa.q: How might Sumit be seeing Chetan's delay?
qa.a: Sumit sees it as fear, not laziness, and gently points out that Sir cannot respond to anything until it is submitted.

grounding: A student leaves the final polish and submission undone for weeks because finishing exposes the work to judgment.

passage:
My design portfolio sat at ninety percent for five weeks, and I told everyone it was almost ready. Truthfully it needed one page redone and a photo of the last project. I could have done both in an evening. But sending it meant Yusuf, my lab-mate, would read it, and then a stranger at the studio would, and someone might say it wasn't good enough. So I reorganised the folders, changed the font twice, and once cleaned my whole desk. It wasn't laziness. I was frightened. One night at 1 a.m. I finally exported the file, wrote a two-line email and clicked send before I could argue. Yusuf's reply came in the morning: “Nice. Second page is my favourite.” I laughed at how heavy the wait had been.
— Lokesh

qa.q: How long did the portfolio sit at ninety percent?
qa.a: The portfolio sat at ninety percent for five weeks.

qa.q: What was Lokesh really feeling while reorganising folders and changing fonts?
qa.a: Lokesh was frightened that the portfolio might be judged not good enough, and the busywork was a way to avoid sending it.

qa.q: What choice did Lokesh make at 1 a.m., and what followed?
qa.a: Lokesh exported the file, wrote a short email and sent it, and the reply the next morning was kind.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel receiving the portfolio?
qa.a: Yusuf was probably glad to be trusted with it and pleased by the work, judging from the reply, “Nice. Second page is my favourite.”

grounding: A student leaves a nearly finished piece unsent for weeks, hiding fear of judgment behind polishing.

passage: Bilal's final design portfolio for his course in Berlin had been ninety percent finished since March. Twelve projects, all laid out. Only the captions, a cover page and the upload to the school portal remained. It was now May. Every Sunday he opened the file, changed a font, then closed it. His flatmate Astrid finally asked, "What's actually left?" He listed it: two hours of work, maybe three. "So why not tonight?" Bilal went quiet. "Because then the tutors will see it. Right now it's still good in my head." Astrid nodded slowly. "Upload it by Friday, and I'll buy the pizza." He wrote the captions that night, hands a little cold.

qa.q: How many projects were in Bilal's portfolio?
qa.a: There were twelve projects.

qa.q: What was Bilal really afraid of?
qa.a: He was afraid of the tutors judging it; while unsubmitted, it stayed good in his head, so avoiding the last steps protected him from that fear.

qa.q: What helped Bilal finally act, and why?
qa.a: Astrid asked what was actually left and set a Friday deadline with a small reward, which made the last two or three hours concrete and shared.

qa.q: How does Astrid see Bilal's weekly font-changing?
qa.a: Astrid seems to see through it gently, guessing it is not laziness, and offers support instead of teasing.

grounding: Shows a student leaving the final polish and submission undone for weeks because finishing means being judged.

passage: The electronics lab at the engineering college was almost empty in the vacation. Karthik sat by the soldering bench with his final-year project report, a smart irrigation sensor. The circuit worked. The report was written. What remained was the formatting, the references and his guide's signature. That had been true for five weeks. Disha, the lab assistant, looked over. "Still here, Karthik? I thought you submitted in June." He laughed awkwardly. "Just checking the graphs again." Disha set down her tray. "Checking or hiding?" His smile faded. "What if Sir reads it and says it's weak?" "Then he'll say it, and you'll fix it. Right now it can't even be weak." Karthik opened the references page.

qa.q: What was Karthik's final-year project?
qa.a: It was a smart irrigation sensor.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when Disha asked, "Checking or hiding?"
qa.a: He felt exposed and anxious, afraid that his guide would call the report weak.

qa.q: What would you advise Karthik to do next?
qa.a: Finish the formatting and references in one sitting and take the report for the guide's signature, accepting that any criticism can be fixed.

qa.q: How does Disha see Karthik's five weeks of checking?
qa.a: Disha sees it as avoidance rather than care, and nudges him kindly with a direct question.

grounding: A student leaves the last formatting and submission undone for weeks, and a lab assistant sees the fear underneath.

passage:
Dear Yusuf sir,

I owe you an honest update. The short film you mentored me on is done except the colour correction, the credits and the festival form. It has been that way since the first week of August.

I told myself I was busy. The truth is I've watched it thirty times and each time I'm more scared. Once I send it, the jury will decide if it's any good. Right now I can still believe it is.

I have booked the editing room for Saturday. If I can finish the credits there, I'll submit on Sunday night. Could I send you the link before I do?

Thank you for not giving up on me,
Damini

qa.q: What three things were left on Damini's film?
qa.a: The colour correction, the credits and the festival form were left.

qa.q: How does Damini feel each time the film is watched again?
qa.a: Damini feels more scared each time, afraid of the jury deciding the film is not good.

qa.q: Which step in the letter makes finishing more likely?
qa.a: Booking the editing room for Saturday and naming Sunday night for submission turn a vague intention into a fixed plan.

qa.q: How might Yusuf sir feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Yusuf sir is likely relieved and touched by Damini's honesty, and glad to see the film before it goes out.

grounding: A student admits in a letter to leaving the final polish and submission undone for weeks out of fear of being judged.

passage:
Irawati, you keep asking why I never sent my story to the college writing contest. Okay. I'm Ritu, and here's the truth.
The story was done by early January. Three thousand words, a proper ending, even a title I liked. All it needed was one last read for typos and the submission form. Maybe an hour.
I didn't do it for five weeks. I told you I was busy. I told myself the ending needed "something." I opened the file twice and closed it without reading.
The contest closed on 10 February. On the 11th I finally read it. It was good. There were four typos. That's all.
What I was actually avoiding was the moment it became real. While it sat at ninety-nine percent, it was a brilliant story in my head. Once I sent it, strangers could say it was bad.
This year, I've put the submission date in my calendar two weeks early. And you're allowed to nag me.

qa.q: How many typos did the story have?
qa.a: There were four typos.

qa.q: What was Ritu really afraid of?
qa.a: Ritu was afraid of judgment, of strangers saying the story was bad once it was submitted.

qa.q: What has Ritu changed for this year, and why might it help?
qa.a: Ritu put the submission date two weeks early in the calendar and asked Irawati to nag, adding a push past the fear.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel hearing this?
qa.a: Irawati might feel sad that the story missed the contest, but glad Ritu is being honest and willing to be nagged.

grounding: Illustrates a student who leaves a nearly finished story unsubmitted for weeks, avoiding the judgment that finishing would bring.
